content: The medication cycloserine is typically prescribed as part of a multi-drug regimen for the treatment of tuberculosis (TB) and, in some cases, urinary tract infections (UTIs). It is not a first-line treatment and is used in combination with other medications. The initial dosage is 250 mg taken orally every 12 hours for 14 days. After this, the maintenance dose ranges from 500 mg to 1 g per day, divided into two doses every 12 hours, with a maximum daily dose of 1 g. For patients with impaired kidney function, the dosing interval should be adjusted based on creatinine clearance (CrCl) levels. For CrCl between 50–80 mL/min, the medication should be administered every 12–16 hours. For CrCl between 10–49 mL/min, the interval should be extended to every 24–36 hours. For CrCl less than 10 mL/min, the medication should be given every 36–48 hours. Cycloserine works by inhibiting bacterial cell wall synthesis and is absorbed at a rate of 70–90%. It is metabolized in the liver, has a half-life of approximately 10 hours in individuals with normal kidney function, and is primarily excreted in the urine (60–70%). Patients should be aware of potential side effects, which include headache, dizziness, drowsiness, tremors, confusion, restlessness, vertigo, cardiac arrhythmias, folate deficiency, hyperreflexia, dysarthria, somnolence, paresis, seizures, coma, and increased liver enzymes. Rare but serious side effects include hypersensitivity reactions, heart failure, and central nervous system (CNS) toxicity, such as depression, psychosis, or seizures. Prolonged use may lead to fungal or bacterial superinfections, including Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea. Cycloserine may interact with other medications, such as ethionamide and isoniazid, which can increase CNS toxicity and the risk of seizures. It may also reduce the effectiveness of sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid by altering metabolism. Patients should avoid alcohol, as it can exacerbate dizziness, drowsiness, and the risk of seizures. Additionally, live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine, may not work effectively while taking this medication. During pregnancy, cycloserine should only be used if clearly needed, as it falls under Pregnancy Category C. It passes into breast milk but is unlikely to harm a nursing infant. Patients should inform their healthcare provider of any allergies, history of seizures, severe anxiety, psychosis, alcoholism, anemia, or impaired liver or kidney function before starting treatment. To minimize side effects, your doctor may recommend taking vitamin B6 (pyridoxine). It is important to take the medication at evenly spaced intervals and complete the full prescribed course, even if symptoms improve. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is close to the next scheduled dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. The medication should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and not in the bathroom. Unused or expired medication should be properly discarded. In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention by calling 911 or a poison control center. Regular medical and laboratory tests, such as sputum tests, blood levels of cycloserine, kidney and liver function tests, and complete blood counts, are recommended during treatment.
